course.learn: High availability designs services to remain accessible despite failures. It uses redundancy, failover, load balancing, clustering, replication, resilient power, and removal of single points of failure.
course.why: The goal is not merely fast recovery after an outage; it is to minimize or avoid service interruption.
course.example: Two application nodes run in separate availability zones behind a load balancer so one zone can fail without taking down the service.
course.exam: Availability clues: redundancy, clustering, failover, load balancing, geographically separated resources, UPS/generator.

course.learn: Load balancing distributes incoming work across multiple systems. Clustering coordinates multiple nodes to provide a service with redundancy and failover.
course.why: Both improve availability, but they solve slightly different problems: workload distribution versus coordinated service resilience.
course.example: A load balancer sends new web requests across three servers; a database cluster elects another node if the active node fails.
course.exam: Load balancer = spread traffic. Cluster = nodes cooperate for resilient service.
